introduction-the-limits-of-configuration.core: HCL and YAML are configuration languages: great for declaring resources, awkward for real abstraction (complex conditionals, loops over nested data, types, unit tests, IDE refactoring). AWS CDK, CDKTF and Pulumi let you define infrastructure in general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, Go, C#), with classes, packages and tests, while still producing a declarative desired state.

first_principles.problem: A Terraform module grows dozens of nested ternaries and dynamic blocks to express simple business rules.

analogy.title: Writing a novel in a spreadsheet vs a word processor
analogy.story: Spreadsheets can hold text, but chapters, styles and search are far easier in the right tool.
analogy.breaks: Novels have no runtime; infra code must stay deterministic.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Abstraction and loops in normal code.

points: Real languages add abstraction and tests.

check.q: What must remain true even when writing IaC in a general-purpose language?
check.a: The program must deterministically produce a declarative desired state; no side effects or randomness at synth time.

aws-cdk-constructs-and-levels.core: In AWS CDK everything is a construct, arranged in a tree under an App and Stacks. L1 constructs (Cfn*) map 1:1 to CloudFormation resources; L2 constructs add sensible defaults and helper methods (bucket.grantRead(role)); L3 patterns bundle several resources into an architecture (ApplicationLoadBalancedFargateService). `cdk synth` renders the tree to CloudFormation templates and `cdk deploy` runs them.

first_principles.problem: A team writes raw CfnBucket everywhere and still hand-writes IAM policies.
derivation: Drop to **L1/escape hatches** for unsupported props.

analogy.title: Raw ingredients, prepared components, and meal kits
analogy.story: Flour (L1), ready pastry (L2) and a complete pie kit (L3): use the highest level that fits.
analogy.breaks: Meal kits can't be tweaked much; L3s allow overrides via escape hatches.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: ALB, service, task def, SGs and IAM from a few lines.

check.q: When would you use an L1 construct?
check.a: When you need a property or new resource type that L2 doesn't yet support, giving direct CloudFormation control.

custom-constructs-encoding-organizationa.core: A custom construct is a class that wraps lower-level constructs with your organisation's rules baked in: encryption, tags, logging, alarms and naming. Teams consume it like any library from an internal package registry, and you can enforce standards across the tree with Aspects that visit every construct (for example to fail synth if a bucket is unencrypted).

first_principles.problem: Every team configures logging and alarms differently, and audits keep finding gaps.
truths: Aspects can enforce across a tree.

analogy.title: A company template for slide decks
analogy.story: Fonts, logos and disclaimers are built in; people just add content.
analogy.breaks: Templates can be ignored; Aspects can fail the build.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Standards by default, violations fail synth.

check.a: A visitor applied to every construct in a scope, used to modify or validate them, e.g. failing synth on non-compliant resources.

cross-stack-references.core: Splitting a CDK app into stacks (network, data, app) and passing an object from one to another makes CDK create a CloudFormation Export in the producer and an Fn::ImportValue in the consumer. Exports are locked while imported, so you can't change or remove them without first removing the consumer: the 'deadly embrace'. For loose coupling, pass values via SSM parameters or look them up by name.

first_principles.problem: Renaming a bucket in the data stack fails because the app stack still imports its old export.
derivation: Pass **construct references** within one app for convenience.
Break the embrace with **exportValue()** two-step deploys.

analogy.title: A signed contract between departments
analogy.story: Once accounting relies on your account number, you can't change it until they agree to stop using it.
analogy.breaks: Contracts can be renegotiated live; exports need ordered deployments.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No CloudFormation export lock between stacks.

check.a: A producer can't remove or change an export while a consumer imports it, but the consumer change can't deploy first because of the dependency order.

pulumi-multi-cloud-with-real-languages.core: Pulumi runs your program (TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, Java or YAML) with an engine that registers resources, diffs them against the stack's state and calls providers directly, without generating CloudFormation. It supports AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes and more in one program. Outputs are async values (Output<T>) resolved after creation, stacks hold per-environment config, and secrets are encrypted in state.

first_principles.problem: A team needs AWS, Cloudflare and Kubernetes resources in one deployment with shared logic.
truths: Values may be unknown until created.
One engine can drive many providers.

analogy.title: A conductor reading a score
analogy.story: The program is the score; the engine conducts each orchestra section (provider) and waits for one part before cueing the next.
analogy.breaks: Orchestras play once; the engine diffs and only changes what differs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Cloudflare record waits on the S3 endpoint output automatically.

code.text:
import pulumi, pulumi_aws as aws, pulumi_cloudflare as cf
site = aws.s3.BucketV2("site")
web = aws.s3.BucketWebsiteConfigurationV2("web", bucket=site.id,
        index_document={"suffix": "index.html"})
cf.Record("www", zone_id=pulumi.Config().require("zoneId"), name="www",
          type="CNAME", content=web.website_endpoint, proxied=True)
pulumi.export("url", web.website_endpoint)

check.q: Why can't you use a Pulumi Output like a plain string?
check.a: Its value may be unknown until the resource is created, so you must transform it with apply/interpolate to keep dependencies tracked.

custom-providers-extending-iac-to-any-ap.core: When no provider exists, both ecosystems let you extend them. Pulumi offers dynamic providers (CRUD functions written inline in your program) for quick wins and full native providers for reuse; it can also bridge any Terraform provider. CDK has CloudFormation custom resources backed by Lambda and the CloudFormation registry for first-class types. Choose based on reuse, testing and ownership.

first_principles.problem: A deployment must create an API key in an internal SaaS that has no IaC support.
truths: Any CRUD API can be modelled.
Lambda-backed resources need careful error handling.

analogy.title: A universal adapter you build yourself
analogy.story: A rough adapter works for one trip; a proper certified one is worth it if the whole team travels.
analogy.breaks: Bad adapters spark; bad custom resources hang stacks for an hour.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Provider framework handles CFN responses and retries.

check.q: Why use the CDK Provider framework instead of a raw Lambda custom resource?
check.a: It handles the CloudFormation response protocol, timeouts and async polling, avoiding stacks hanging when the Lambda fails to respond.
